newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Feb PPI falls 0.4 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Feb PPI falls 0.4 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported its Producer Price Index (PPI) fell 0.4 percent in February against a 0.3 percent loss in January.
Excluding food and energy, the PPI fell 0.1 percent in February, compared to an unchanged reading in January. Experts had expected PPI to drop 0.1 percent and rise 0.1 in the core.
MARILYN SCHAJA, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DLJ SECURITIES CORP: "This is a very good report and indicates that there is really no inflation to worry about at the producer level."

Schaja continued: "The chances are still in favor that the (Federal Reserve) will move at the March 25 meeting." Fed Chairman Alan "Greenspan told you he wants to be preemptive, so he is not going to wait until inflation shows up in these numbers. I think that it is a difficult call, but I continue to think that based on the labor market, consumer spending numbers ... and Greenspan's comments, the Fed will move."
DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "The weak PPI is broad based.
"It is not affected by any single factor.

Seto went on: "You have a very strong economy, but it is not showing up in any kind of pressures on product prices. This gives the Fed some breathing room. It buys them some time; they can wait until May."

JOHN PARK, ECONOMIST, SANWA SECURITIES (USA) CO: "Basically, this is all energy prices. Energy prices being down 1.2 percent is a bigger decline that what people were looking for. We were expecting a bit of a bounce from capital equipment, but that did not come through.

Park added: "If you look at the crude and intermediate numbers ... this whole thing is pretty much all energy. If you look away from energy, it doesn't look so benign. In pipeline costs, you're probably still going to be seeing the uptrend we've seen for the past six to eight months.

"I'm not particularly sure today's PPI and next week's (Consumer Price Index) is going to play much of a role (in the Fed's decision). The whole point of a preemptive strike is that you're going to move before something really concrete shows up in the price data. Finished goods doesn't show that, but the pipeline costs are trending up."

JOSEPH LIRO, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CIBC WOOD GUNDY SECURITIES: "The inflation numbers are just too tame for (the Fed) to tighten. It really puts them in a dilemma. I think they need at least one bad inflation number before they can pull the trigger and there's nothing in this number that you can point to. You can point to the 1.0 percent increase in core crude goods after the 2.0 percent increase last month, but that's a desperate attempt because the correlation with what's happening at the core crude goods stage and final consumer prices is exceptionally low.
"It's literally verging on the miraculous that we continue to run with robust economic growth but no evidence of inflation and you need that evidence before they can go."
